name: Rice Blast Disease
description: A serious fungal disease affecting rice leaves, nodes, and panicles, often triggered by excessive nitrogen and high humidity.
symptoms: Spindle-shaped or diamond-shaped lesions on leaves with grayish centers and brown borders
Lesions enlarge and coalesce, causing entire leaves to dry and wither
Brownish rot at the neck of the panicle causing lodging and empty grain heads
prevention: Use certified blast-resistant seed varieties (e.g., IR64, Swarna sub-1)
Avoid excessive application of synthetic urea/nitrogen fertilizers
Maintain balanced plant spacing (20cm x 15cm) to ensure proper field ventilation
cure: Apply bio-fungicide spray containing Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 10g/liter of water
Spray copper-based organic formulations (Bordeaux mixture 1%) on infected patches
Drain stagnant water from fields for 2-3 days to lower canopy humidity

name: Wheat Stripe (Yellow) Rust
description: A destructive airborne fungal disease that forms yellow-orange stripe patterns along leaf veins, reducing grain development.
symptoms: Bright yellow-to-orange powdery fungal pustules arranged in parallel lines on leaves
Leaves turn yellow, dry up prematurely, and drop early
Severely shriveled grain development resulting in significant yield loss
prevention: Sow certified rust-resistant wheat varieties (e.g., HD-2967, PBW-550)
Adjust sowing time to early November to avoid peak cool-humid weather during heading
Eradicate wild grasses and volunteer wheat plants along field borders
cure: Spray organic wettable sulfur (3g/liter) early in the morning when dew is minimal
Apply bio-control agents such as Trichoderma harzianum to soil and foliage
Isolate and remove heavily infected border rows to reduce airborne spore spread

name: Tomato Early Blight
description: A common fungal leaf spot disease affecting older lower leaves first, commonly spread by soil splash and warm rainy weather.
symptoms: Dark brown to black spots with concentric rings (target board pattern) on lower leaves
Yellow halos surrounding the spots followed by rapid leaf drop
Dark sunken leathery lesions near the stem end of developing fruits
prevention: Practice crop rotation: avoid planting after potatoes, brinjals, or peppers
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead sprinklers to keep foliage dry
Mulch soil surface with clean straw to prevent soil-borne fungal spores from splashing onto lower leaves
cure: Spray neem oil extract (5ml/liter) with mild soap emulsion every 7-10 days
Apply copper oxychloride (2.5g/liter) on lower foliage at the first sign of spots
Prune and safely discard infected lower foliage away from the main field

name: Potato Late Blight
description: An aggressive water-mold disease that rapidly destroys potato foliage and rots tubers during cool, damp weather.
symptoms: Water-soaked dark lesions appearing rapidly near leaf tips and margins
White cottony fungal growth on the underside of leaves in high humidity
Brown, dry rot extending inward under the skin of potato tubers
prevention: Plant certified disease-free seed tubers from trusted agricultural institutes
Hill soil high around the base of potato plants to prevent spores reaching tubers
Ensure wide spacing between ridges for rapid drying of foliage
cure: Spray bio-fungicide Bacillus subtilis or copper hydroxide (2g/liter) immediately
Destroy and burn infected haulms (vines) before harvesting tubers to prevent contact rot
Store harvested tubers in a cool, dry, well-ventilated space and discard any soft-rot tubers
